claim: Polarity establishment in many cells is thought to occur via positive feedback that reinforces even tiny asymmetries in polarity protein distribution.
source: Polarity establishment in many cells is thought to occur via positive feedback that reinforces even tiny asymmetries in polarity protein distribution.
evidence: This is a statement about established scientific understanding in the field, supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Cdc42 and related GTPases are activated and accumulate in a patch of the cortex that defines the front of the cell.
source: Cdc42 and related GTPases are activated and accumulate in a patch of the cortex that defines the front of the cell.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in cell biology supported by extensive literature.

claim: Positive feedback enables spontaneous polarization triggered by stochastic fluctuations.
source: Positive feedback enables spontaneous polarization triggered by stochastic fluctuations, but as such fluctuations can occur at multiple locations, how do cells ensure that they make only one front?
evidence: This is a theoretical framework supported by modeling and experimental work in the field.

claim: In polarizing cells of S. cerevisiae, positive feedback can trigger growth of several Cdc42 clusters at the same time.
source: In polarizing cells of the model yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, positive feedback can trigger growth of several Cdc42 clusters at the same time, but this multi-cluster stage rapidly evolves to a single-cluster state, which then promotes bud emergence.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the authors' experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: The multi-cluster stage rapidly evolves to a single-cluster state, which then promotes bud emergence.
source: In polarizing cells of the model yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, positive feedback can trigger growth of several Cdc42 clusters at the same time, but this multi-cluster stage rapidly evolves to a single-cluster state, which then promotes bud emergence.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the authors' experiments.

claim: Resolution of multi-cluster intermediates occurs through a greedy competition between clusters to recruit and retain polarity proteins from a shared intracellular pool.
source: By manipulating polarity protein dynamics, we show that resolution of multi-cluster intermediates occurs through a greedy competition between clusters to recruit and retain polarity proteins from a shared intracellular pool.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by experimental manipulations and observations.

claim: A migrating leukocyte with two fronts would split itself apart.
source: For some cells, restricting polarity to a single front is absolutely imperative: for example, a migrating leukocyte with two fronts would split itself apart (Houk et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Neurons can grow several neurites simultaneously, each with a front-like tip.
source: However, other cells routinely specify more than one front: for example, neurons can grow several neurites simultaneously, each with a front-like tip (Dotti et al., 1988).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: GFP-tagged Cdc42 is not fully functional.
source: Because GFP-tagged Cdc42 is not fully functional (Freisinger et al., 2013; Howell et al., 2012; Watson et al., 2014), we adapted a strategy recently shown to produce a functional internal mCherry-tagged Cdc42 in S. pombe (Bendezu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Internal mCherry-tagged Cdc42 was not fully functional in S. cerevisiae at single copy.
source: Although more functional than GFP-Cdc42 at single copy, this probe was still not fully functional in S. cerevisiae (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 1A,B.

claim: Bem1 is a scaffold protein that participates in positive feedback.
source: Bem1 is a scaffold protein that participates in positive feedback (Kozubowski et al., 2008) and accumulates at the same sites as Cdc42 with very similar timing (Howell et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Bem1 accumulates at the same sites as Cdc42 with very similar timing.
source: Bem1 is a scaffold protein that participates in positive feedback (Kozubowski et al., 2008) and accumulates at the same sites as Cdc42 with very similar timing (Howell et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: When a losing cluster disassembles, Cdc42 and Bem1 disappear in concert.
source: when a losing cluster disassembles, Cdc42 and Bem1 disappear in concert (Figure 1C) (Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1C and Video 1.

claim: Spa2 is a regulator of the formin Bni1, which nucleates actin cables.
source: Spa2 is a regulator of the formin Bni1, which nucleates actin cables (Evangelista et al., 2002; Sagot et al., 2002; Sheu et al., 1998)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Spa2 recruitment to the polarity site occurs via both actin-dependent and actin-independent routes.
source: Spa2 recruitment to the polarity site occurs via both actin-dependent and actin-independent routes (Ayscough et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Sec4 is a secretory vesicle-associated Rab-family GTPase, which polarizes as vesicles are delivered on actin cables to the polarity site.
source: Sec4 is a secretory vesicle-associated Rab-family GTPase, which polarizes as vesicles are delivered on actin cables to the polarity site (Mulholland et al., 1997; Schott et al., 2002; Walch-Solimena et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Spa2-mCherry and GFP-Sec4 both became detectable at the polarity site within about 1 min after Bem1 became detectable.
source: Spa2-mCherry and GFP-Sec4 both became detectable at the polarity site within about 1 min after Bem1 became detectable (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative imaging data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: When cells formed two polarity clusters, Spa2 and Sec4 generally accumulated at both sites.
source: We found that when cells formed two polarity clusters, Spa2 and Sec4 generally accumulated at both sites (Figure 2C) (Video 2).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2C and Video 2.

claim: Both the 'winner' and the 'loser' recruited vesicles (and presumably actin cables), indicating that actin cable recruitment does not guarantee persistence of the polarity cluster.
source: That is, both the 'winner' (W) and the 'loser' (L) recruited vesicles (and presumably actin cables), indicating that actin cable recruitment does not guarantee persistence of the polarity cluster.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that both clusters recruit vesicles but only one persists.

claim: Actin cables are unlikely to act as the hypothesized stabilizer.
source: Hence, actin cables are unlikely to act as the hypothesized stabilizer.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that both winning and losing clusters recruit actin cables.

claim: Actin patches clustered at the polarity site several minutes after Bem1 became detectable.
source: Actin patches were initially distributed randomly around the cortex (with some concentration at the old cytokinesis site), and then clustered at the polarity site several minutes after Bem1 became detectable (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: In most cells that formed two polarity clusters, actin patches remained randomly distributed until one of the clusters had disappeared.
source: In most cells that formed two polarity clusters, actin patches remained randomly distributed until one of the clusters had disappeared (Figure 2E) (Video 3).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2E and Video 3.

claim: Neither the winner nor the loser accumulated actin patches during the relevant timeframe, so actin patches are unlikely to act as the stabilizer.
source: As neither the winner nor the loser accumulated actin patches during the relevant timeframe, actin patches are also unlikely to act as the stabilizer.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that actin patches do not accumulate at either cluster during competition.

claim: Septins assembled into a ring around the polarity site several minutes after Bem1 became detectable.
source: Septins assembled into a ring around the polarity site several minutes after Bem1 became detectable (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: In cells that formed two polarity clusters, septins were not readily detectable at either cluster until after one cluster disappeared in most cells.
source: In cells that formed two polarity clusters, septins were not readily detectable at either cluster until after one cluster disappeared in most cells (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Septins were occasionally detected at both clusters before one cluster disappeared.
source: However, we occasionally detected septins at both clusters before one cluster disappeared (Video 4).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Video 4.

claim: Septins seem unlikely to act as the stabilizer.
source: Thus, septins also seem unlikely to act as the stabilizer.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that septins do not consistently distinguish winning from losing clusters.

claim: Septins contribute to negative feedback and cluster destabilization by recruiting Cdc42-directed GAPs.
source: Indeed, it has been suggested that septins contribute to negative feedback and cluster destabilization by recruiting Cdc42-directed GAPs (Okada et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Polarity factors exchange dynamically between the cluster and the cell interior on a 2–4 s timeframe.
source: Indeed, fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP) experiments indicate that polarity factors exchange in and out of clusters on a 2–4 s timeframe (Freisinger et al., 2013; Slaughter et al., 2009; Wedlich-Soldner et al., 2004)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous FRAP studies.

claim: Multi-cluster resolution occurs on a 1–2 min timeframe.
source: whereas multi-cluster resolution occurs on a 1–2 min timeframe (Howell et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: In the absence of Rdi1, exchange of Cdc42 in and out of the polarity cluster was much slower.
source: We confirmed previous reports (Freisinger et al., 2013; Slaughter et al., 2009) that in the absence of the sole yeast Rho-GDI, Rdi1, exchange of Cdc42 in and out of the polarity cluster was much slower (Figure 3B,C)
evidence: This is supported by FLIP and FRAP data shown in Figure 3B,C and citations to previous work.

claim: Levels of total Cdc42 were similar in wild-type and rdi1Δ cells.
source: while levels of total Cdc42 were similar in wild-type and rdi1Δ cells (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Cdc42 was able to exchange between different lipid vesicles in vitro even in the absence of a GDI.
source: Biochemical experiments indicated that Cdc42 was able to exchange between different lipid vesicles in vitro even in the absence of a GDI (Johnson et al., 2009)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous biochemical work.

claim: There was a substantial pool of Cdc42 in the cytoplasm of rdi1Δ mutants lacking a GDI.
source: and there was still a substantial pool of Cdc42 in the cytoplasm of rdi1Δ mutants lacking a GDI, as detected either by fractionation (Tiedje et al., 2008) or fluorescence correlation spectroscopy (Das et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work using different methods.

claim: Bem1-GFP-CAAX cells do not require the formin Bni1.
source: Unlike Bem1-Snc2, however, we found that Bem1-CAAX did not require the formin Bni1 (Figure 4B,C)
evidence: This is supported by tetrad dissection and microscopy data shown in Figure 4B,C.

claim: Bem1-CAAX does not require F-actin in order to polarize.
source: or F-actin (Figure 4D) in order to polarize.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data showing polarization in the presence of Latrunculin A (Figure 4D).

claim: The finding that Bem1-CAAX polarizes in the absence of Bni1 or F-actin implies that its mobility is not dependent on actin-mediated vesicle traffic.
source: The finding that Bem1-CAAX polarizes in these situations implies that its mobility is not dependent on actin-mediated vesicle traffic.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that Bem1-CAAX polarizes without actin.

claim: Rapamycin led to a rapid loss of detectable Bem1-CAAX from the polarity site in all cells.
source: We found that rapamycin led to a rapid loss of detectable Bem1-CAAX from the polarity site in all cells (Figure 4E)
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The polybasic-prenyl motif slows but does not eliminate membrane-cytoplasm exchange.
source: In aggregate, these experiments indicate that the polybasic-prenyl motif slows but does not eliminate membrane-cytoplasm exchange
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experiments including FLIP, FRAP, and anchor-away assays.

claim: Strains in which Cdc24-CAAX replaced endogenous Cdc24 exhibited very poor viability.
source: Strains in which Cdc24-CAAX replaced endogenous Cdc24 exhibited very poor viability (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by tetrad dissection data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: A mostly nonphosphorylatable Cdc2438A-CAAX was viable.
source: Indeed, a mostly nonphosphorylatable Cdc2438A-CAAX was viable (Figure 5A), although the cells were slower-growing and temperature-sensitive (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by tetrad dissection and growth assay data shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: Cells in which Bem1-CAAX replaced Bem1 were fully viable and grew well at all temperatures.
source: In contrast, cells in which Bem1-CAAX replaced Bem1 were fully viable and grew well at all temperatures (Figure 5B)
evidence: This is supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Cdc2438A-CAAX and Bem1-CAAX were expressed at comparable levels to Cdc24 and Bem1, respectively.
source: Cdc2438A-CAAX and Bem1-CAAX were expressed at comparable levels to Cdc24 and Bem1, respectively (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence quantification data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Bem1-CAAX displayed stronger plasma membrane association than Bem1.
source: Bem1-CAAX displayed stronger plasma membrane association than Bem1 (Figure 5D)
evidence: This is supported by cortical to internal fluorescence ratio data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Bem1-CAAX exchange in and out of the polarity site was slower than that of Bem1, as assessed by FLIP or FRAP.
source: and Bem1-CAAX exchange in and out of the polarity site was slower than that of Bem1, as assessed by FLIP or FRAP (Figure 5E,F).
evidence: This is supported by FLIP and FRAP data shown in Figure 5E,F.

claim: Bem1-CAAX clusters grew more slowly than Bem1 clusters, and failed to show the characteristic overshoot before reaching their final intensity.
source: Bem1-CAAX clusters grew more slowly than Bem1 clusters, and failed to show the characteristic overshoot before reaching their final intensity (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Membrane-cytoplasm exchange of Bem1 can (when slowed) become rate-limiting for the growth of polarity clusters.
source: This finding suggests that membrane-cytoplasm exchange of Bem1 can (when slowed) become rate-limiting for the growth of polarity clusters.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that Bem1-CAAX clusters grow more slowly.

claim: When two or more polarity clusters formed in any of the slow-exchange strains, the clusters tended to persist for prolonged periods compared to wild-type cells.
source: When two or more polarity clusters formed in any of the slow-exchange strains, the clusters tended to persist for prolonged periods compared to wild-type cells (Figure 6A–D).
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 6A-D.

claim: Average coexistence intervals changed from ~1.5 min in control strains to ~7 min in slow-exchange strains.
source: Quantification revealed a heterogeneous range of coexistence times, with average intervals changing from ~1.5 min in control strains to ~7 min in slow-exchange strains (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Both the growth and competition intervals were longer in slow-exchange strains than in wild-type controls.
source: Both the growth and competition intervals were longer in slow-exchange strains than in wild-type controls (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Slowing the exchange of polarity factors extended the time necessary to resolve multi-cluster intermediates, consistent with a model in which clusters compete for shared components.
source: Thus, slowing the exchange of polarity factors extended the time necessary to resolve multi-cluster intermediates, consistent with a model in which clusters compete for shared components.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that slow-exchange strains have prolonged competition.

claim: In several cases both winning and losing clusters acquired septin rings.
source: In several cases both winning and losing clusters acquired septin rings (Figure 7A) (Video 5).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 7A and Video 5.

claim: The presence of septins did not prevent cluster disassembly, and the septin ring also disappeared when a cluster lost the competition.
source: However, the presence of septins did not prevent cluster disassembly, and the septin ring also disappeared when a cluster lost the competition (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The authors never observed disassembly of a septin-containing cluster in cells that did not have another cluster present (n>200).
source: Because we never (n>200) observed disassembly of a septin-containing cluster in cells that did not have another cluster present, it would appear that septin disassembly does not occur spontaneously
evidence: This is a direct observation from the authors' experiments.

claim: The disappearance of 'losing' clusters is due to the presence of another cluster, consistent with the competition hypothesis.
source: and therefore that the disappearance of 'losing' clusters is due to the presence of another cluster, consistent with the competition hypothesis.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that septin-containing clusters only disassemble when another cluster is present.

claim: In all of the slow-exchange strains, cells that formed two buds at the same time were encountered.
source: In all of the slow-exchange strains, we also encountered cells that formed two buds at the same time (Figure 7B,C) (Video 6).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 7B,C and Video 6.

claim: Both buds always emerged at about the same time.
source: Buds could be similar (Figure 7B, cell 1; 7C, cell 1) or dissimilar (Figure 7B, cells 2,3; 7C, cell 2) in size, but both buds always emerged at about the same time.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 7B,C.

claim: The size difference between buds does not arise because one bud gets a head start.
source: This observation indicates that the size difference does not arise because one bud gets a head start
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that buds emerge simultaneously.

claim: In cases with different-sized buds, competition had proceeded to form unequal clusters at the time of bud emergence, giving one bud a growth advantage.
source: rather, in those cases with different-sized buds competition had proceeded to form unequal clusters at the time of bud emergence, giving one bud a growth advantage.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation of unequal bud sizes emerging simultaneously.

claim: In a few cases, the smaller bud ceased growing.
source: In a few cases, the smaller bud ceased growing (Figure 7B, cells 2,3), suggesting that competition continued even after bud emergence, leaving an abandoned bud.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The authors never saw a bud stop growing in cells that had only a single bud (n>200).
source: We never (n>200) saw a bud stop growing in cells that had only a single bud, suggesting that abandonment of the bud is due to competition with another bud.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the authors' experiments.

claim: The presence of actin and septin structures is unable to stabilize a cluster against competition.
source: These findings indicate that the presence of actin and septin structures is unable to stabilize a cluster against competition, arguing strongly against the stabilizer hypothesis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from observations that clusters with actin and septins can still lose competition.

claim: Combining rdi1Δ with BEM1-CAAX is lethal with CDC2438A-CAAX.
source: We were able to combine rdi1Δ mutants with either Cdc2438A-CAAX or Bem1-CAAX, but combination of Cdc2438A-CAAX with Bem1-CAAX proved lethal (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is supported by tetrad dissection data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: rdi1Δ BEM1-CAAX strains displayed multibudded cells at increased frequency.
source: rdi1Δ BEM1-CAAX strains displayed multibudded cells at increased frequency (Figure 8B)
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The frequency of multibudded cells in viable strains rose to almost 40%.
source: The frequency of multibudded cells in viable strains rose to almost 40% (Figure 8B)
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Some cells grew three or four buds simultaneously.
source: and some cells grew three or four buds simultaneously (Figure 8C-E) (Video 7).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 8C-E and Video 7.

claim: In a few instances the smallest bud ceased growing, suggesting that competition can continue after bud emergence.
source: As discussed above, in a few instances the smallest bud ceased growing, suggesting that competition can continue after bud emergence.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from observations of abandoned buds.

claim: Multibudded cells generated anucleate or aneuploid progeny.
source: Imaging slow-exchange strains carrying a fluorescent histone revealed that multibudded cells generated anucleate (Figure 8F, cell 1) or aneuploid (Figure 8F, cells 2 and 3) progeny
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 8F.

claim: In aneuploid progeny, a mother and bud appeared to fight over the daughter nuclei.
source: in which a mother and bud appeared to fight over the daughter nuclei (Video 8).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Video 8.

claim: A computational model based on the behavior of the core polarity factors displays competitive behavior.
source: In summary, a computational model based on the behavior of the core polarity factors displays competitive behavior because a larger peak has advantages both in terms of reducing diffusional losses and improved recruitment and retention of factors from the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is a conclusion from computational modeling described in the manuscript.

claim: A larger peak has advantages in terms of reducing diffusional losses and improved recruitment and retention of factors from the cytoplasm.
source: In summary, a computational model based on the behavior of the core polarity factors displays competitive behavior because a larger peak has advantages both in terms of reducing diffusional losses and improved recruitment and retention of factors from the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is a conclusion from computational modeling.

claim: In a cell with unequal polarity clusters, the largest will grow at the expense of the others.
source: Thus, in a cell with unequal polarity clusters, the largest will grow at the expense of the others.
evidence: This is a conclusion from computational modeling.

claim: Substrate depletion from the cytoplasm ultimately stops clusters from growing further.
source: As polarity factors are recruited to one or more peaks, the cytoplasmic levels of the polarity factors decline, and it is this substrate depletion from the cytoplasm that ultimately stops clusters from growing further.
evidence: This is a conclusion from computational modeling.

claim: Once a single peak has been consolidated, the levels of cytoplasmic factors are too low to support a second peak.
source: Thus, once a single peak has been consolidated, the levels of cytoplasmic factors are too low to support a second peak.
evidence: This is a conclusion from computational modeling.

claim: In CDC2438A mutants, polarity clusters showed competition on similar timescales as that observed in wild-type cells.
source: In CDC2438A mutants, polarity clusters showed competition on similar timescales as that observed in wild-type cells (Kuo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: In CDC2438Ardi1Δ mutants, slow competition and formation of two-budded cells were observed.
source: Moreover, in CDC2438Ardi1Δ mutants we observed slow competition and formation of two-budded cells (Figure 10A).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 10A.

claim: Cells that made a single bud developed polarity clusters with a higher polarity protein content than those in cells that made two buds.
source: As predicted by the substrate depletion scenario, cells that made a single bud developed polarity clusters with a higher polarity protein content than those in cells that made two buds (Figure 10B).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 10B.

claim: Competition in cells lacking negative feedback proceeds in a manner consistent with the critical features of the model: insatiable positive feedback combined with substrate depletion.
source: Thus, competition in cells lacking negative feedback proceeds in a manner consistent with the critical features of the model: insatiable positive feedback combined with substrate depletion.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from observations in CDC2438A mutants.

claim: Negative feedback does not greatly affect the competition process in yeast cells.
source: The observation that competition proceeds similarly after eliminating a major negative feedback pathway suggests that negative feedback does not greatly affect the competition process in yeast cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from observations in CDC2438A mutants.

claim: The authors detected multiple polarity clusters as an intermediate stage in polarity establishment in approximately 50% of cells under their imaging conditions.
source: We detected multiple polarity clusters as an intermediate stage in polarity establishment in approximately 50% of cells under our imaging conditions (see also Howell et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the authors' experiments.

claim: Two-fold reductions in polarity factor abundance reduced the incidence of multi-cluster intermediates considerably.
source: In addition, there may be strain background differences in multi-cluster frequency, as we found that two-fold reductions in polarity factor abundance reduced the incidence of multi-cluster intermediates considerably.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data on hemizygous strains.

claim: Hemizygotes contained half as much Cdc42 or Cdc24 as homozygotes.
source: Western blotting showed that hemizygotes contained half as much Cdc42 or Cdc24 as homozygotes (Figure 11F).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 11F.

claim: Multi-cluster intermediates were detected in about 50% of wild-type cells, 25% of CDC24 hemizygotes, and 5% of CDC42 hemizygotes.
source: Whereas we detected more than one initial cluster in about 50% of wild-type cells, multi-cluster intermediates were detected in only 25% of CDC24 hemizygotes and 5% of CDC42 hemizygotes (n>100 cells for each strain) (Figure 11G).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 11G.

claim: No multi-cluster instances were observed in cells doubly hemizygous for both CDC42 and CDC24 (n=73).
source: No multi-cluster instances were observed in cells doubly hemizygous for both CDC42 and CDC24 (n=73) (Figure 11G).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 11G.

claim: Multiple clusters are less frequent in cells that express lower levels of polarity factors.
source: Thus, multiple clusters are less frequent in cells that express lower levels of polarity factors.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from observations in hemizygous strains.

claim: The uniqueness of the yeast front is due to competition for polarity factors, and not to a downstream stabilizer.
source: Our findings suggest that uniqueness of the yeast front is due to competition for polarity factors, and not to a downstream stabilizer.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: The speed of competition can be manipulated by altering the rates at which key polarity factors exchange between membrane and cytoplasm.
source: We show that the speed of competition can be manipulated by altering the rates at which key polarity factors exchange between membrane and cytoplasm
evidence: This is a conclusion from experiments with slow-exchange mutants.

claim: Cells with slowed competition can maintain multiple fronts for long enough to make two, three, or even four buds simultaneously.
source: and that cells with slowed competition can maintain multiple fronts for long enough to make two, three, or even four buds simultaneously.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data of slow-exchange mutants.

claim: Mutations in a plant GDI gene lead to the frequent production of multiple growing root hair sites in a single cell.
source: Strikingly, mutations in a plant GDI gene lead to the frequent production of multiple growing root hair sites in a single cell (Carol et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work in plants.

claim: Competition between polarity sites for Rop2 may ensure that only one root hair grows per cell.
source: We speculate that competition between polarity sites for Rop2 may ensure that only one root hair grows per cell.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on analogy to yeast findings.

claim: Slowing the exchange of Rop2 may impair competition in the plant root hair system, allowing more than one site to initiate tip growth.
source: By analogy to our findings for yeast, slowing the exchange of Rop2 may impair competition in that system, allowing more than one site to initiate tip growth.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on analogy to yeast findings.
